1:3: Paul speaks of God’s word as if it were an object that could be visibly shown to people.
Paul assumes that his readers will understand that the proclamation refers to the message of the gospel of Jesus Christ.
1:4: Though Titus was not Paul’s biological son, they share a common faith in Christ. Paul considers relationship to Christ through faith to be more important than biological relationship. Thus, because of their relative ages and shared faith in Christ, Paul considers Titus as his own son. It may also be that Paul led Titus to faith in Christ, and so Titus is like a son in this spiritual sense.
1:6: This is the beginning of the description of the character of an elder. Paul assumes that Titus understands that he is to choose men who fit the following description.

This means that he has only one wife; that is, he does not have any other wives or concubines. This also means that he does not commit adultery and may also mean that he has not divorced a previous wife.
This could refer to: (1) children who believe in Jesus; (2) children who are trustworthy.
1:7: The word overseer is another name for the same position of spiritual leadership that Paul referred to as “elder” in 1:5. This term focuses on the function of the elder: he oversees the activities and people of the church.
Paul speaks of the church as if it were God’s household, and the overseer as if he were a servant in charge of managing that household.
1:8: Here Paul is speaking of what is good as if it were a person who could be someone’s friend.
The terms sensible and self-controlled are very similar in meaning and may be translated by one term if the target language does not have two similar terms.
The terms righteous and holy are very similar in meaning and may be translated by one term if the target language does not have two similar terms.
1:9: Paul speaks of devotion to the Christian faith as if it were grasping the faith with one’s hands.
The word translated here as sound normally refers to being physically healthy. Paul is speaking of this teaching as if it were a living thing that could be healthy or sick.
1:10: Here, empty is a metaphor for useless, and empty talkers are people who say useless or foolish things.
The word deceivers describes people who are actively trying to convince people to believe in something other than the true gospel that Paul preaches.
Both empty talkers and deceivers refer to the same people, those who are also rebellious. Those people taught false, worthless things and wanted other people to believe them.
Here, circumcision represents the Jewish believers who taught that men must be circumcised in order to please God. This teaching is false.
1:11: The implication is that these people must be stopped from teaching.
The issue was that they were leading families away from the truth and destroying their faith.
Here Paul refers to profit as shameful, meaning that the activity of accepting money for teaching wrong things brings shame on the teacher.
1:12: The word always here is an overstatement for emphasis.
This metaphor is speaking of Cretans as if they were evil beasts.
Here the part of the body that stores food is used to represent the person who eats all the time.
1:14: Paul speaks of the truth as if it were an object that one could turn away from or avoid.
1:15: Here, Paul uses or invents a proverb in order to teach that being pure or pleasing to God is a matter of a person’s inward thoughts, not a matter of outward actions or rituals.
τοῖς δὲ μεμιαμμένοις καὶ ἀπίστοις, οὐδὲν καθαρόν
Paul speaks of sinners as if they were physically corrupted or dirty.
2:1: Here, you is singular and refers to Titus.
See the note about sound teaching on Titus 1:9.
2:2: These three words are very close in meaning and may be combined into one or two terms if the target language does not have three separate terms.
ὑγιαίνοντας τῇ πίστει, τῇ ἀγάπῃ, τῇ ὑπομονῇ
Here the word sound means to be firm and unwavering. It applies to faith, love, and perseverance. See the note about sound on Titus 1:9 and the note about sound in faith on Titus 1:13.
2:3: People who cannot control themselves and drink too much wine are spoken of here as if they were a slave to the wine.
2:6: Paul’s instructions for the different groups of believers are similar.
2:7: It is possible that this phrase is part of the previous sentence instead of this one.
2:8: Here the word sound applies to Titus’s message and means “accurate” or “correct,” as it does in Titus 1:9 and 2:1 where it also applies to teaching.
This presents a hypothetical situation in which someone opposes Titus and then becomes ashamed for having done so.
2:9: The implication is that the slaves are to be pleasing to their masters.
2:10: The implication is that they would be tempted to steal from their masters.
2:11: Paul speaks of the grace of God as if it were a person who has arrived.
Here the word salvific describes God’s grace, meaning that it is like a person who has the characteristic of saving people.
2:12: Paul speaks of the grace of God (2:11) as if it were a person who trains other people how to live holy lives.
2:13: τὴν μακαρίαν ἐλπίδα, καὶ ἐπιφάνειαν τῆς δόξης
These two phrases connected with and express a single event. The words blessed hope describe how Paul feels about the appearing of Jesus.
τοῦ μεγάλου Θεοῦ καὶ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν, Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ
Both our great God and Savior refer to the one person, Jesus Christ.
2:14: Here, Paul speaks of lawlessness as though it were an evil master from whom Jesus sets us free.
2:15: Here, these things refers back to all of the things that Paul has said in chapter two.
Paul assumes that Titus understands that he should exhort the believers to obey these things.
If it is helpful, the people whom Titus should rebuke can be made explicit.
The way that people would disregard Titus could be made explicit.
3:1: The words submit and obey have very similar meanings and both refer to doing what someone tells you to do. If the target language has only one term for this, then just use that term.
The words rulers and authorities have similar meanings and both refer to anyone who holds authority in the government. If the target language has only one term for this, then just use that term.
3:3: πλανώμενοι, δουλεύοντες ἐπιθυμίαις καὶ ἡδοναῖς ποικίλαις
Here, passions and pleasures are spoken of as if they were masters over people and had made those people into slaves by lying to them.
3:4: Paul speaks of God’s kindness and love as if they were physical things that came into our sight.
3:5: Paul combines two metaphors here. He is speaking of God’s forgiveness for sinners as if he were physically washing them clean from their sin. He is also speaking of sinners who become responsive to God as if they experience a new birth.
3:6: It is common for New Testament writers to speak of the Holy Spirit as a liquid that God can pour out in large amounts.
3:7: Here, that one refers back to “our Savior Jesus Christ” in verse 6.
κληρονόμοι γενηθῶμεν, κατ’ ἐλπίδα ζωῆς αἰωνίου
The people to whom God has made promises are spoken of as if they were to inherit the things promised, just as a person inherits property or possessions from a family member.
3:8: This message is the one just expressed in verses 4–7, that God freely gives the Holy Spirit and eternal life to believers through Jesus.
Here, these things refers to the teachings that Paul has talked about in verses 1–7.
3:9: The word genealogies refers to the study of family kinship relationships. See the Introduction to Titus for more information. Paul assumes that Titus will understand that he means for Titus to avoid arguing about genealogies.
Paul assumes that Titus will understand that he is referring to the law of Moses, not Roman law.
3:10: The implication is that this person is causing division in the church.
The implication is that Titus should warn the person who is causing division.
3:11: Paul speaks of someone who chooses to do wrong things as if he were leaving the right path to walk in the wrong direction.
3:12: ὅταν πέμψω Ἀρτεμᾶν πρὸς σὲ ἢ Τυχικόν
The implication is that Titus should come to Nicopolis after either Artemas or Tychicus arrives to where Titus is.
3:13: The implication here is that to Diligently send these men is to help and equip them.
3:14: Here essential needs refers to things that people must have in order to live.
Paul speaks of people doing good work as if they were trees bearing good fruit.
3:15: Here, in faith is an idiom that refers to those who share the same faith.
This was a common Christian greeting and is also a blessing.
